item.title: Narazuke: Nara's Amber Sake-Lees Pickles — Guide
item.description: Narazuke are Nara’s celebrated sake-lees pickles, one of the city’s oldest food traditions, dating back over a thousand years to when temple brewers preserved vegetables in the fragrant lees (kasu) left over from making sake. Melon, cucumber, ginger, gourd and other vegetables are repeatedly re-pickled in fresh sake lees over months or even years, slowly turning a deep translucent amber and taking on a complex, richly aromatic flavour — sweet, savoury, and distinctly boozy.

item.title: Funazushi: Japan's Oldest Sushi, Fermented on Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Funazushi is the ancestor of all sushi: nigorobuna carp from Lake Biwa, salted and then buried in cooked rice to ferment for one to three years, a preservation method over a millennium old from which modern sushi eventually evolved. The result is nothing like the sushi the world knows — the flesh turns dense, tangy and creamy, with an aroma often compared to strong cheese — and it remains a proud, polarising delicacy cured by family houses around the lake, served sliced with the golden fermented rice, floated in hot broth as ochazuke, or nibbled alongside local sake, which flatters it best.

item.title: Shinshu Miso: Japan's Most Widely Produced Miso — Guide
item.description: Shinshu miso, the rice-based miso produced in Nagano, is Japan’s most widely made variety, accounting for around half of all the country’s miso production, thanks to the region’s cool climate being ideal for the slow fermentation that gives it its characteristic golden colour and balanced, medium-salty flavour. Beyond seasoning countless dishes, the miso can be explored at breweries around the prefecture, some historic and centuries old, which offer tours, tastings and shops explaining the fermentation process behind this staple of Japanese cooking.

item.title: Mishima-machi Kouji Pickles: A Fermented Mountain Craft — Guide
item.description: Mishima-machi, a small mountain village in the Aizu region, is known for kouji-zuke — vegetables pickled and fermented using rice kouji (the mould culture also used in sake and miso production), a preservation tradition passed down through generations of local households to survive the region’s long, snowbound winters. The result is a mildly sweet, umami-rich pickle distinct from vinegar-based tsukemono, sold at farm stands, local markets and specialty shops throughout the village.

item.title: Sendai Miso: A Bold Red Miso with Samurai Roots — Guide
item.description: Sendai miso is a distinctive dark red, unpasteurised soybean paste with a bold, slightly bitter depth of flavour, aged for over a year in wooden vats. Its origins trace to the early 1600s, when warlord Date Masamune established a dedicated miso brewery to supply his troops with long-lasting, nutritious rations — making it one of Japan’s oldest continuously produced regional misos. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Sendai, Miyagi Hours Shop hours; some breweries offer tours Admission Free tasting at many shops; miso from ~¥500 Time needed 30–45 min Best time Year-round What to Try Rich miso soup made with Sendai miso at local restaurants.
